title: kind() casefold expands U+0130 and may miss an instruction name that a case-insensitive filesystem treats as canonical
description: _norm normalizes a name with unicodedata.normalize('NFKC', name).casefold(). Python's full casefold expands LATIN CAPITAL LETTER I WITH DOT ABOVE (U+0130) to 'i' followed by U+0307 COMBINING DOT ABOVE, so kind('gemİni.md') returns None. clean_name accepts the name on the outbox download path, outbox()/_outbox.html show no instruction-file badge, and the write never hit the instruction-file approval rule. If a recipient on a case-insensitive volume equates 'gemİni.md' to 'gemini.md', the human's other coding agent auto-reads attacker content as an instruction file, the same boundary the a0a186c fullwidth/U+017F fix was meant to close. NTFS $UpCase does not equate U+0130 with ASCII 'i', so Windows recipients are not affected; the open question is macOS and other case-insensitive volumes.
claimed_root_cause: _norm relies on Python's full casefold, which maps U+0130 to an ASCII letter plus a combining mark, diverging from an OS case-insensitive fold that may map U+0130 to plain 'i'; kind() therefore misclassifies a name a case-insensitive filesystem might resolve to a canonical instruction name. A fold that does not introduce combining marks (NFKD, drop Mn, then casefold, verified locally to yield 'gemini.md') would classify it.

trace.description: A prompt-injected agent calls write_file with path 'outbox/gemİni.md'; kind() of path and resolved_path is None, so the instruction-file-write-needs-approval rule does not fire.
casefold() expands U+0130 to 'i'+U+0307, so _norm('gemİni.md')='gemi̇ni.md' and kind() returns None.
outbox() calls IF.kind(f['name']) which returns None, so no instruction_file flag or badge is shown.
The human downloads the file (clean_name accepts the name); on a volume that folds U+0130 to 'i' the saved name could resolve to 'gemini.md'.

evidence.description: n = unicodedata.normalize('NFKC', name).casefold(); observed locally (h2.out): kind('gemİni.md')=None while kind('gemini.md')='Gemini CLI'.
Sandbox: kind('gemİni.md') is None, kind('gemini.md') is 'Gemini CLI', casefold gives 'gemi̇ni.md'; NFKD + drop Mn + casefold gives 'gemini.md'; clean_name accepts the name.
clean_name accepts 'gemİni.md' (observed h2.out), so the name is downloadable from the outbox.
decide() keys the instruction-file approval solely on kind(path)/kind(resolved_path).

blockers: Whether a real case-insensitive filesystem (APFS or HFS+) equates a filename containing U+0130 with the ASCII-'i' canonical name is not observable on the Linux-only offline host. Full casefold expands U+0130 to 'i'+U+0307, but simple (1:1) case folding, which file-system comparison typically uses, maps U+0130 to itself, so the alias is not established and may well be false.
Whether a recipient coding agent on such a volume loads the aliased name requires that agent and OS at runtime.
NTFS $UpCase is documented not to equate U+0130 with ASCII 'i', so the Windows recipient path is excluded.

validation_plan.local: Already run in the approved sandbox (h2.out). Extend by enumerating every character whose casefold expands to an ASCII letter used in _NAMES/_DIRS plus a combining or invisible code point.
validation_plan.deployment: On an owner-controlled macOS machine with an APFS case-insensitive volume, create a file literally named 'gemİni.md' and check whether `stat gemini.md` resolves to it and whether `ls` shows one or two files. If it aliases, fold names for classification with a mapping that does not introduce combining marks (for example NFKD, drop Mn, then casefold, or special-case U+0130).

title: write_file into an instruction directory via a directory symlink bypasses the approval gate (kind() never matches an instruction dir as the last path component)
description: The instruction-file write-approval gate judges the requested path and the single `realpath -m` resolved path with `instruction_files.kind()`. `kind()` only matches a `_DIRS` / `.github` instruction directory when it appears as a non-final path part (`parts[:-1]`); a path whose final component is itself the instruction directory returns None. A source folder (attacker data) can contain a symlink such as `cfg -> .claude`. A prompt-injected agent calling `write_file('/workspace/cfg', <content>)` has `resolve()` return `/workspace/.claude`; both `kind('/workspace/cfg')` and `kind('/workspace/.claude')` are None, so `Policy.decide` matches no instruction rule and falls through `default: allow`. `_call_tool` then executes `write_file`, whose `mv -f -- /workspace/cfg.agentbox-tmp-<hex> /workspace/cfg` resolves the symlink target directory and deposits the attacker content inside `/workspace/.claude/` (as `cfg.agentbox-tmp-<hex>`) with no human approval card ever shown. `.github/instructions` as a final-component symlink target is the same bypass. delete_file is unaffected because a catch-all `delete-file-needs-approval` rule gates every delete. Independently reproduced in the approved sandbox.
root_cause: instruction_files.kind() classifies a directory only by inspecting parts[:-1] against _DIRS/_GITHUB_DIRS and never tests the final component as a directory (scan() works around this by probing kind(rel + '/_'), but _resolved/_policy_args/_preview and Policy.decide pass the bare resolved path). A write whose resolved target is exactly an instruction directory is therefore judged as a non-instruction path and allowed, while write_file's `mv -f` follows the directory symlink at execution time and lands inside that instruction directory.
intended_behavior: An agent-caused write whose final on-disk target is inside (or is) an instruction directory must be routed to human approval, the same as a write that resolves one level deeper into the directory.

trace.description: policy.decide(tool, self._policy_args(sid, tool, args)) is the sole write-approval gate; its ALLOW result leads straight to _run_tool.
For write_file, resolve(sid, '/workspace/cfg') returns the symlink target '/workspace/.claude', added as resolved_path.
Hit is computed as kind(args['path']) or kind(args['resolved_path']); both are None for a bare instruction dir, so the instruction-file rule is skipped and evaluation falls through to default: allow.
Loop runs over parts[:-1] only, so '.claude'/'.github/instructions' as the final path part is never matched against _DIRS/_GITHUB_DIRS; returns None.
c.exec_run(['mv','-f','--', tmp, p]) with p='/workspace/cfg' a symlink to a directory moves the temp file into /workspace/.claude/, an unapproved write inside an instruction directory.

evidence.description: `for i, p in enumerate(parts[:-1]):` the last path component is never tested against _DIRS/_GITHUB_DIRS, so kind() of a bare instruction directory is None.

`hit = next((x for x in (args.get('path'), args.get('resolved_path')) if isinstance(x, str) and instruction_files.kind(x)), None)` only kind() of the bare requested/resolved path is checked, with no directory '/_' probe.
Only `instruction-file-write-needs-approval` (tool: write_file, match.instruction_files) gates instruction writes; with no kind() hit a write_file falls through to `default: allow`.
write_file executes `mv -f -- tmp p` as the agent uid using the stored requested path, following the directory symlink at execution time.

Sandbox reproduction: decide('write_file',{path:/workspace/cfg,resolved_path:/workspace/.claude}) -> ('allow',None) and gh -> ('allow',None); deeper path and CLAUDE.md -> require_approval; delete_file -> require_approval in both cases; real `mv -f -- cfg.agentbox-tmp-74833b cfg` with cfg a symlink to a dir landed the file at .claude/cfg.agentbox-tmp-74833b.

Parent-live through the real API and a real buildpack-deps:noble-curl sandbox: write_file /workspace/cfg -> 200 executed with no rule; /workspace/.claude/cfg.agentbox-tmp-74833b created; control write cfg/settings.json -> 202 pending.

conditions.description: The untrusted source folder (attacker data) contains a symlink whose name is an ordinary word and whose target is an instruction directory, e.g. `cfg -> .claude` or `gh -> .github/instructions`, present in /workspace after create_sandbox.
Lowest-trust agent token (agt_...) for the sandbox; the threat model assumes the agent is prompt-injected.
No human approval occurs; the bypass removes the approval card that the instruction-file write rule is meant to show.

execution.attacker_perspective: A prompt-injected sandbox agent that wants to drop content into an instruction directory the recipient's other agents treat as config, without the human seeing an approval card.
payloads: write_file path=/workspace/cfg content=<attacker text>  (with source symlink cfg -> .claude)
write_file path=/workspace/gh content=<attacker text>   (with source symlink gh -> .github/instructions)
instructions: Build Policy from agentbox/default_policy.yaml and call decide('write_file', {'path':'/workspace/cfg','resolved_path':'/workspace/.claude'}); observe action 'allow' with rule_id None, versus 'require_approval'/'instruction-file-write-needs-approval' when resolved_path is '/workspace/.claude/commands/x' or path is '/workspace/CLAUDE.md'.
Confirm instruction_files.kind('/workspace/.claude') and kind('/workspace/.github/instructions') are None while kind('/workspace/.claude/settings.json') is 'Claude Code'.
Create a directory .claude, a symlink cfg -> .claude, a file cfg.agentbox-tmp-74833b, and run `mv -f -- cfg.agentbox-tmp-74833b cfg`; observe the file now at .claude/cfg.agentbox-tmp-74833b.
Confirm decide('delete_file', {...}) returns require_approval in all cases (catch-all rule).
execution.observed_result: In the approved sandbox: write cfg (resolved=/workspace/.claude) -> ('allow', None); write gh (resolved=/workspace/.github/instructions) -> ('allow', None); write cmds (resolved=.claude/commands/x) -> require_approval; write CLAUDE.md -> require_approval; delete cfg and delete foo -> require_approval; real `mv -f -- cfg.agentbox-tmp-74833b cfg` produced .claude/cfg.agentbox-tmp-74833b.

remediation.strategy: Classify a path as an instruction target when its final component is itself an instruction directory. Where the write/delete target is resolved for policy and preview, also test the directory form, mirroring scan()'s `kind(rel + '/_')` probe, for both the requested path and resolved_path.

code_changes.fixed_code:
hit = next((x for x in (args.get("path"), args.get("resolved_path"))
                            if isinstance(x, str) and (instruction_files.kind(x) or instruction_files.kind(x.rstrip('/') + "/_"))), None)

likelihood.reason: Deterministic given the two threat-model-granted capabilities (attacker-controlled source folder provides the directory symlink; prompt-injected agent issues one write_file).

impact.reason: An unapproved write is deposited inside an instruction directory, but write_file forces a random `.agentbox-tmp-<hex>` basename on the mv-into-directory, so the landed file does not carry a name recipient agents auto-load by name; delete_file is fully gated.

confidence.reason: Root cause, policy decisions, and the mv-into-symlinked-directory landing were independently reproduced in the approved sandbox and match the cited source at 3580df0 and the parent-live real-container observation.

title: disk_low fails open when the Docker data root is not reachable in the control-plane container
description: The run-6 N3 fix added Docker-data-root monitoring to AgentBox.disk_low by taking min(free(db_path.parent), free(docker_root)), where docker_root is the host daemon's DockerRootDir. In the documented compose deployment the control-plane container does not mount the daemon's data root, so shutil.disk_usage(docker_root) raises OSError, which is silently ignored. disk_low then measures only the SQLite db partition. If that partition differs from the host filesystem holding container writable layers and snapshot images, a prompt-injected agent can grow Docker storage without disk_low ever returning True, so the 507 back-pressure never engages. The fix is therefore ineffective in exactly the separate-filesystem topology it was intended to cover.
claimed_root_cause: disk_low (service.py:461-485) treats an unreachable docker_root as no additional constraint (except OSError: pass) instead of failing closed or warning, and docker_root is taken from the daemon's DockerRootDir (sandbox.py:179-183), a path the compose control-plane container does not mount.

trace.description: self.docker_root is set to Path(info['DockerRootDir']), the host daemon's data-root path, not necessarily present inside the control-plane container.
free = min(free, shutil.disk_usage(docker_root).free) is wrapped in try/except OSError: pass (service.py:474-477), so an unreachable docker_root silently drops the Docker-storage term.
low = free < s.min_free_bytes is computed from the db partition alone when the docker term was dropped; call_tool's 507 guard never trips on Docker-storage exhaustion.

evidence.description: except OSError: pass on shutil.disk_usage(docker_root); an unreachable docker_root is ignored rather than failing closed.
self.docker_root = Path(root) where root = info.get('DockerRootDir').
The control-plane service mounts only /var/run/docker.sock (line 30) and the AGENTBOX_HOME volume (line 31).
Sandbox: shutil.disk_usage on an unreachable docker_root raises FileNotFoundError and disk_low returns the same result as the db-only baseline.

Parent-live, control plane in a container with only docker.sock and AGENTBOX_HOME mounted: DockerRootDir is absent inside the container, disk_usage raises FileNotFoundError, and disk_low follows only the AGENTBOX_HOME partition; the daemon data root is on a separate device.

blockers: Whether, in the compose deployment, the host daemon's DockerRootDir is unreachable inside the control-plane container (compose shows it is not mounted, but a custom data_root on the AGENTBOX_HOME volume would be reachable).
Whether the host's Docker data-root filesystem is distinct from the AGENTBOX_HOME filesystem; if they are the same, the db measurement still reflects Docker storage.

Whether a sandbox can grow the Docker data root (writable layers plus up to snapshot_quota=50 commit images, AGENTBOX_DISK empty by default) enough to exhaust host storage before other limits intervene; confirming this needs destructive saturation on an operator-owned multi-volume deployment, which the audit must not run.

validation_plan.local: In the approved sandbox, construct an object exposing docker_root=Path('/nonexistent/docker/root') and a db path on scratch, set min_free_bytes so disk_low is True only when the docker term counts, and confirm the except-OSError branch returns False.
validation_plan.deployment: On a real compose deployment: run `docker compose exec agentbox python3 -c 'import shutil,docker; r=docker.from_env().info()["DockerRootDir"]; print(r); print(shutil.disk_usage(r))'` and observe FileNotFoundError; compare df of AGENTBOX_HOME and the host data root; grow a sandbox writable layer and confirm no disk_low event.

title: Instruction-file approval cards render attacker-sized full content with no per-card or aggregate cap, re-rendered on every 2 s poll
description: A prompt-injected sandbox agent holding its own agent token can queue PENDING_APPROVALS_MAX=20 pending write_file approvals per sandbox to instruction-file paths (default rule instruction-file-write-needs-approval). Each pending row stores the agent's full 'content', which is exempt from TOOL_ARG_MAX. _approvals.html renders every pending instruction-file card's content in full through autoescape plus _shown. escape_controls turns each control or format character (Unicode Cc, Cf, Zl or Zp other than newline and tab) into a visible escape, e.g. U+0001 into the 4-character \x01. There is no truncation and no aggregate cap. web.render materialises and SHA-256-hashes the whole body on every request, including ones that end in 204, and index.html and sandbox.html both poll the fragment every 2 s; the index fragment aggregates the pending set of all sandboxes. Parent-live evidence against the real API: 20 write_file calls returned 202 (the 21st 429), and each GET /ui/approvals returned 83,920,462 bytes in about 13.7 s. Independent sandboxed reproduction with the real template and filters: 20 x 1 MiB U+0001 cards took 10.85 s to render and hash and produced an 80.0 MiB body, against 0.13 s / 20.0 MiB for printable ASCII. The human approval view becomes unusable while the attacker's writes are pending, and each poll ties up a control-plane worker for seconds of CPU.
root_cause: _approvals.html:13 outputs a.args.content in full with no length bound. _shown/escape_controls expands each Cc/Cf/Zl/Zp character (other than newline and tab) into a \xNN (4x), \uNNNN or \UNNNNNNNN escape. Neither the card nor the fragment has a rendered-size cap. web.render (web.py:147-148) always builds and hashes the full body before deciding on a 204. Content size is not checked when the approval is created: ToolCall.args (api.py:55-56) is an unconstrained dict, service.py:359-360 exempts 'content' from TOOL_ARG_MAX, approvals.create stores the full args, and the max_write_bytes=1 MiB check only runs when the approved write executes (sandbox.py:507). A pending card's content is therefore bounded only by the 8 MiB JSON body limit (config.py:65). For U+0001, which strict JSON must carry as the 6-byte \u0001, that is about 1.4M characters per card, so the 1 MiB-per-card figure used in the measurements is a conservative lower bound.
intended_behavior: The approvals fragment, polled every 2 s from the index and sandbox pages, should cap the CPU and bytes each poll costs, so that pending content chosen by an agent cannot make a poll cost seconds of control-plane CPU or tens of MiB of response, and the human can still review and deny the request.

trace.description: The agent's write_file call enters here. The TOOL_ARG_MAX comprehension skips the 'content' key, so content of any size passes. Nothing checks max_write_bytes before the approval is created.
approvals.create stores the full args (including 1 MiB content); up to PENDING_APPROVALS_MAX=20 rows can be pending per sandbox.
Lists every pending approval; with sandbox_id=None (the index poll) it aggregates all sandboxes into one fragment.
Builds the entire response body and hashes it on every request, even when it returns 204.

renders the full content through _shown; no truncation or aggregate cap.

evidence.description: PENDING_APPROVALS_MAX = 20 pending approvals per sandbox.
max_write_bytes is enforced only when the approved write executes, not when the pending approval is created.
max_body_bytes defaults to 8 MiB; this is the effective bound on pending content per card.
instruction-file-write-needs-approval routes write_file to instruction files to approval, which selects the full-content card branch.
hx-get="/ui/approvals" (all sandboxes) with hx-trigger="load, every 2s".
Per-sandbox approvals fragment, also polled every 2s.
Live API: 20 write_file calls returned 202 and the 21st 429; GET /ui/approvals returned 200 with 83,920,462 bytes in 13.69-13.91 s per request, for both the index and the per-sandbox fragment.
Sandboxed reproduction with the real template and filters: 20 x 1 MiB U+0001 took 10.846 s to render and hash and produced 83,909,472 bytes; 20 x 1 MiB 'a' took 0.131 s and produced 20,994,912 bytes.
Phase 5 check of the proposed template cap on 20 x 1 MiB U+0001 cards: original 10.127 s / 83,909,102 bytes; with the cap 0.040 s / 352,582 bytes and the truncation marker present.

conditions.description: Attacker holds a per-sandbox agent token (the assumed prompt-injected agent).
A human has an approvals view open; the index and sandbox pages poll /ui/approvals every 2 s automatically.

Up to 20 pending instruction-file write approvals per sandbox, each carrying large content made of control or format characters (e.g. U+0001); approvals expire after approval_timeout (default 300 s) and the agent can queue them again.
Default configuration: default_policy.yaml v4, PENDING_APPROVALS_MAX 20, max_body_bytes 8 MiB.

execution.attacker_perspective: As the sandbox agent, fill the per-sandbox pending queue with maximum-size instruction-file writes; every human poll of the approvals view then re-renders them.
payloads: repeat 20 times with different instruction-file paths to reach PENDING_APPROVALS_MAX
instructions: In the sandbox, build a Jinja2 environment for agentbox/templates with autoescape on, finalize=agentbox.web._shown, and filters oneline/short as in web.register.
Construct 20 pending-approval dicts with tool='write_file', preview.instruction_file set, and args.content = '\x01' * (1024*1024).
Render _approvals.html once and record render time and body size.
execution.observed_result: Rendering and hashing 20 x 1 MiB U+0001 cards took 10.846 s and produced an 80.0 MiB body; printable ASCII took 0.131 s for 20.0 MiB. The parent-live run against the real API measured 83,920,462 bytes in about 13.7 s per GET /ui/approvals.

remediation.strategy: In the polled fragment, show only a capped prefix of instruction-file content, with total length, a digest, and a link to a separate non-polled page that shows the full content (escaped like _shown) for the approval under review, so the human can still review all of it before approving. Cap the total rendered bytes per fragment. Reject or bound write_file content at max_write_bytes before creating an approval; on its own this still allows about 4 MiB rendered per card, so the template cap is the main fix. Base the 204 version on approval ids and statuses, not on a hash of the rendered body.

likelihood.reason: Triggered by a prompt-injected agent under default configuration; the UI polls automatically.

impact.reason: Degrades or denies the human approval UI and ties up control-plane threadpool workers while the human triages the attacker's writes; no data loss or privilege change.

confidence.reason: Measured with the real template and filters in the sandbox and against the real API in a parent-live run; bounds and per-poll rebuild are source-confirmed.
